t: Count No-Zero Pairs That Sum to N — Digit DP on Carries
o: We must count ordered pairs (a, b) of positive integers with no digit 0 anywhere, such that a + b = n. In example 1 (n = 2), only (1,1) works; in example 2 (n = 3), (1,2) and (2,1) both count because pairs are ordered; in example 3 (n = 11), any pair containing a number with a 0 (like 10) is excluded, leaving 8 pairs. Since n can be up to 10^15, iterating over all candidate values of a is hopeless (~10^15 iterations), so we need something proportional to the number of *digits*, i.e. about 16. The natural tool is a digit-by-digit construction of a and b from the least significant digit upward, tracking the carry — a classic digit DP.
k: Build a and b digit by digit from the least significant end; at each position the chosen digits plus the incoming carry must match the corresponding digit of n.
A number 'contains a 0' refers only to its written digits, so leading padding zeros are harmless: once a number has started (taken a nonzero digit), it can never take a 0 again.
The whole state is just (position, carry, startedA, startedB), giving at most 16 × 2 × 2 × 2 states with 100 digit-pair transitions each.

a.i: For each a from 1 to n-1, set b = n - a and check whether both a and b avoid the digit 0. This directly mirrors the definition and is trivially correct. Checking a value is O(log n) via repeated division by 10. It is far too slow for n near 10^15, but serves as the conceptual baseline and passes small constraints.
s: Define a helper ok(x) that returns true iff x has no digit 0 (repeatedly take x % 10 and x //= 10).
For each a in [1, n-1], let b = n - a.
If ok(a) and ok(b), increment the answer.
a.t: O(n log n) — one pass over all a with an O(log n) digit check each; infeasible for n up to 10^15.

a.n: Approach 2: Digit DP over Carries and Started Flags (Optimal)
a.i: Construct a and b simultaneously from the least significant digit of n upward. At position i with incoming carry c, pick digits x (for a) and y (for b) with (x + y + c) mod 10 equal to digit d_i of n; the outgoing carry is floor((x + y + c)/10). A digit 0 for a number is legal only while that number has not yet started (it is just leading padding); once started, only digits 1–9 are allowed. At the end we require the final carry to be 0 (otherwise the sum exceeds n) and both numbers to have started (both positive). The state space is tiny, so memoized recursion runs instantly even for 10^15.
s: Extract the digits of n least-significant-first into an array.
Define dp(i, c, sa, sb): number of ways to finish positions i..end given incoming carry c and started flags sa, sb.
For each x, y in 0..9 with (x + y + c) % 10 == digits[i]: skip if (x == 0 and sa) or (y == 0 and sb); recurse with carry (x + y + c) // 10 and updated flags sa or x > 0, sb or y > 0.
Base case i == len(digits): return 1 iff c == 0 and sa and sb.
a.t: O(L · 2^3 · 100) where L ≤ 17 is the digit count of n — about 13,600 transition checks, effectively constant time.
a.sp: O(L · 2^3) for the memo table plus O(L) recursion depth.

w: In an interview, mention the brute force first to show you understand the problem, then immediately pivot to the digit DP once you note n can be 10^15. The critical pitfalls are: (1) forgetting that pairs are ordered — (1,2) and (2,1) count separately, which the DP handles naturally since a and b play distinct roles; (2) mishandling leading zeros — a shorter number like 2 paired against 11 is legal, so digit 0 must be permitted before a number 'starts', but forbidden afterward; (3) requiring the final carry to be 0 so the sum has exactly the digits of n; (4) requiring both flags true at the end so neither number is zero. Edge cases: smallest input n = 2 (answer 1), powers of 10 like n = 11 vs n = 10 (any pair summing to 10 needs a trailing-zero interaction — the DP resolves it correctly). Likely follow-ups: count unordered pairs (divide by symmetry considerations carefully), or extend to three summands (add another digit dimension and started flag).
